Statistical physics

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 85k Articles: 980
Statistical physics explains collective behavior using probability distributions over microscopic possibilities. Its central surprise is that incomplete microscopic knowledge can still produce precise predictions for internal energy, entropy and heat capacity. The bridge is statistical mechanics: specify the available microstates, assign their probabilities, then compute the expected values of measured quantities.
A two-level system already displays the idea. Warming it makes its higher energy more likely; its heat capacity first rises, then falls as the two probabilities approach equality. With two distinguishable units, merely counting microstates explains why the middle energy has twice the state degeneracy. These small examples expose the machinery before the much larger sums needed for a photon gas or an Ising model.
The appeal is economical: the same microscopic energies and probabilities explain both an average reading and its variance. A measurement's spread therefore becomes useful physical information rather than an inconvenience to discard.

Mean-field theory

Words: 44
Statistical physics OurBigBook.com
Mean-field theory replaces fluctuating interactions with a self-consistent average field. For example, an Ising spin feels a field determined by the average neighboring spin magnetization; a self-consistency equation approximates the interacting Ising model. Neglecting correlated fluctuations can fail near a continuous phase transition. The mean-field approximation in Landau theory is a particular use of this general framework.

Thermal fluctuation (⟨(δA)2⟩=kB​T∂h​⟨A⟩)

Words: 51
Statistical physics OurBigBook.com
A thermal fluctuation is the randomness of an observable in an equilibrium Boltzmann distribution. If the energy contains −hA, differentiation of its partition function gives ∂h​⟨A⟩=β(⟨A2⟩−⟨A⟩2). Thus the fluctuation variance is related to the response to a conjugate source. In a field theory, the two-point version is the connected correlation function.

Photon gas

Words: 1k Articles: 1
Statistical physics OurBigBook.com
A photon gas is a collection of photons described statistically as radiation. Here the equilibrium model is homogeneous, isotropic electromagnetic radiation in vacuum at temperature T>0: each photon has energy E=c∣p∣=hν, with momentum p and frequency ν, and there are two independent transverse states of electromagnetic polarization. An absorbing cavity with walls at a common temperature provides a way to establish this thermal equilibrium. The bulk formulas assume cavity dimensions much larger than the typical wavelength hc/(kB​T), so the electromagnetic mode density in a box can replace individual cavity modes by a continuum. [ref]
The crucial constraint is whether photon emission and photon absorption, or other number-changing processes, can equilibrate the photon population. When they can, photon number is not an independently conserved quantity and the equilibrium photon chemical potential is μγ​=0. For each polarization and frequency, the mean occupation number then follows the Bose-Einstein distribution:
f(ν)=exp[hν/(kB​T)]−11​.
(1)
If number-changing processes are ineffective but number-conserving interactions redistribute energy, a constrained Bose-Einstein distribution can instead have f=[exp((hν−μγ​)/(kB​T))−1]−1 with chemical potential μγ​≤0 fixed by the number constraint. Thus thermal equilibrium with respect to energy exchange alone does not establish μγ​=0. The zero value can also persist in an already prepared Planck photon distribution during suitable subsequent evolution; continual photon emission is not required to preserve it. [ref]
Combining f with the two-polarization density of states, gν​/V=8πν2/c3, gives the Planck photon distribution and the spectral photon energy density:
dνdnγ​​=c38πν2​f(ν),uν​≡dνdu​=c38πhν3​f(ν)=c4π​Bν​(T).
(2)
Here Bν​ is the spectral radiance in Planck's law; uν​ is stored energy density per unit frequency, not outgoing power per area. Their different units are connected by the full-sphere solid angle and the speed of light c. The Boltzmann constant is kB​, and h is the Planck constant. [ref]
The equilibrium equation of state is particularly simple:
u=aR​T4,p=3u​,aR​=15h3c38π5kB4​​=c4σ​≃7.565733250×10−16Jm−3K−4.
(3)
The radiation constant aR​ is the same constant called arad​ in black-body radiation; σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. An outline of the energy density calculation substitutes x=hν/(kB​T) and uses ∫0∞​x3/(ex−1)dx=π4/15. The radiation pressure follows because the angular average of the squared directional component of photon momentum is 1/3 for isotropy; the thermodynamic derivation of blackbody radiation pressure supplies an independent route. These formulas describe the radiation contribution, not the cavity walls. The isotropic massless relation p=u/3 survives a different isotropic spectrum, whereas the coefficient in u=aR​T4 requires the zero-chemical potential Planck photon distribution.
For a computed example with stipulated T=2.725K, the photon energy density is u≃4.17174×10−14Jm−3 and the radiation pressure is p≃1.39058×10−14Pa. The photon number density in the International System of Units is
nγ​=16πζ(3)(hckB​T​)3≃4.10501×108m−3,nγ​u​=30ζ(3)π4​kB​T≃2.70118kB​T.
(4)
Here ζ is the Riemann zeta function. The mean photon energy differs from the energy at the peak of a spectral curve: counting photons and weighting them by energy emphasize different frequencies. The calculations use the exact International System of Units values of the Planck constant, Boltzmann constant and speed of light. [ref]
A motivating observation is the cosmic microwave background spectrum measured by the Far Infrared Absolute Spectrophotometer (FIRAS) aboard COBE. Its apparatus used a polarizing Michelson interferometer, with one input viewing a roughly seven-degree sky patch and the other an internal blackbody. Scanning mirrors changed the optical path length difference; heat-sensitive detectors recorded the varying power, and Fourier transform spectroscopy recovered the spectral difference. Operation outside the terrestrial atmosphere removed atmospheric emission and absorption, while shielding and cooling the optics in a helium cryostat suppressed the instrument's own radiation. [ref]
Absolute calibration came from moving an external blackbody into the sky aperture, filling the same beam used for the sky. This was an iron-loaded epoxy absorber shaped as a re-entrant cone. Repeated reflections made it a close approximation to a blackbody, while thermometers supplied its temperature. Mather and colleagues explicitly evaluated reflections, temperature gradients, radiation leaking through the material and leakage around its edge. These are limits on how faithfully the calibrator realizes thermal equilibrium radiation, rather than details that can be eliminated merely by calling it black. [ref]
During sky observations the internal blackbody temperature was adjusted to nearly null the spectral difference, reducing gain and drift errors. Fixsen and colleagues' 1996 analysis used calibrated spectra over wavenumbers 2 to 21cm−1, about 60 to 630GHz. They separated the sky's spatially uniform component, its dipole and Galactic emission, and varied sky cuts and foreground templates as controls. The resulting cosmic microwave background spectrum agreed with a single Planck function, with reported RMS deviations below 50 parts per million of its peak brightness. This is a residual statistic over the analyzed spectrum, not a pointwise relative error bound at every frequency. [ref]
The observation motivates using a photon gas as a physical model rather than merely a formal counting exercise. Its interpretation has a clear boundary: agreement with Planck's law constrains departures from an equilibrium spectral shape within the calibrated band and foreground assumptions; it does not directly measure radiation pressure or entropy density of a photon gas. Nor does it establish that today's cosmic microwave background is continually re-equilibrating with matter. A previously thermal spectrum can retain its Planck function shape as expansion of the universe lowers every photon frequency in the same proportion. The usefulness of the model is that one measured spectral temperature, together with its equilibrium assumptions, predicts energy density, radiation pressure, photon number density and entropy density of a photon gas consistently.

Entropy density of a photon gas (s=4aR​T3/3)

Words: 523
Photon gas OurBigBook.com
The entropy density of a photon gas is its entropy per physical volume, s=S/V. For homogeneous equilibrium vacuum radiation with two states of electromagnetic polarization and zero photon chemical potential,
s=Tu+p​=34​aR​T3,S=34​aR​T3V.
(5)
The first equality is the entropy density at zero chemical potential, obtained from the thermodynamic Euler relation U=TS−pV+μγ​Nγ​ with internal energy U=uV. Statistical mechanics

Words: 150
Statistical physics OurBigBook.com
Statistical mechanics connects microstates to macrostates through probability distributions. Its microcanonical ensemble, canonical ensemble and grand canonical ensemble specify different constraints on exchanges with the surroundings. An ensemble average describes repeated preparations under those constraints; it need not be the value in every individual preparation.
This makes the subject useful whenever tracking every microscopic detail would obscure the question being asked. To predict a heat capacity, we need how the expected value of energy changes with temperature, rather than a record of every unit's state. The partition function packages that calculation into one reusable object.
In his 1902 book, J. Willard Gibbs systematically developed the canonical ensemble. His preface contrasts following one system through time with studying a collection of systems with different microscopic conditions. Chapter IV defines the canonical ensemble through an exponential function of energy and establishes its normalization. This supplied a general strategy for predicting collective measurements by averaging over possible microscopic conditions, with the partition function organizing the calculation. [ref] [ref]

The ergodic hypothesis identifies long-time averages of equilibrium observables along typical trajectories with averages over the invariant equilibrium ensemble at the same conserved quantities. In the microcanonical formulation, the ensemble is normalized phase-space measure on the energy surface. In a measure-preserving description, ergodicity means invariant measurable sets have measure zero or one; the Birkhoff ergodic theorem then equates time averages and ensemble expectations almost everywhere for integrable observables. This explains why statistical-mechanical ensembles can predict long-time measurements. A particular mechanical model still requires its own ergodicity assumptions; integrable idealized systems need not be ergodic.

An ice bath can absorb heat while its temperature barely changes: the heat converts ice into water. The latent heat of fusion quantifies this melting budget. For a pure substance at its equilibrium melting temperature Tm​(p) and specified pressure p, define it here per unit mass:
L(p)=hl​(Tm​(p),p)−hs​(Tm​(p),p),h=H/m.

A molar fusion enthalpy instead has units Jmol−1 and equals ML, where M=m/n is mass divided by amount of substance in kgmol−1. Always check the normalization before inserting a tabulated value into an energy balance.[ref] [ref]
For a closed system converting completely from solid to liquid at fixed pressure, with only pressure-volume work and negligible changes in bulk kinetic energy and potential energy, the first law of thermodynamics gives Qp​=ΔH=mL. Both endpoints are at Tm​(p): warming initially colder ice or subsequently warming the resulting water requires additional sensible heat. Since H=U+pV, the corresponding specific internal energy jump is Δu=L−pΔv, where v=V/m; L includes the work associated with the change in volume. Heat is transferred energy, whereas enthalpy is a state function. [ref]

The final warming takes another 4.18kJ. Weigh the container and stirrer, then weigh the added warm water to obtain mw​. Let the container and water reach a common initial temperature Ti​. Add it without splashing, stir gently, and record temperature before addition and until after the last ice disappears. Reweigh to find the added mass mi​. The left side supplies the fusion enthalpy and the sensible heat on the right; the water produced by melting must be warmed too. Superconductivity is a phase of matter that supports steady electric current with zero bulk electrical resistivity and exhibits the Meissner effect: equilibrium screening of a sufficiently weak, static magnetic field from the interior. It occurs below a material-dependent superconducting transition temperature, provided the electric current and applied magnetic field are also sufficiently small. [ref] Bulk expulsion means that a sample much thicker than its London penetration depth has an almost field-free interior; the magnetic field need not vanish at its surface. Conventional BCS theory explains superconductivity through correlated Electrons forming Cooper pairs. [ref]
The two observations answer different questions. A resistance-versus-temperature experiment for superconductivity asks whether a steady electric current requires a measurable electric potential difference. A Field-cooled Meissner experiment asks whether a magnetic field already present in the material is expelled when it enters superconductivity. An ideal perfect conductor with zero electrical resistivity can preserve that pre-existing magnetic field; zero electrical resistance alone therefore does not establish the Meissner effect.
The usefulness follows directly from Joule heating, P=I2R: maintaining a steady electric current through a segment with zero electrical resistance produces no resistive heating in that segment. This makes persistent electric currents attractive for producing steady magnetic fields. The beauty is that one phase has both a transport property and an equilibrium magnetic response, and the second cannot be inferred just by making an ordinary electrical resistance very small. The London equations encode this extra magnetic response. [ref]

The Field-cooled Meissner experiment starts above the superconducting transition temperature with a weak, steady applied magnetic field already penetrating a solid sample. Meissner and Ochsenfeld reported magnetic expulsion in 1933, showing that the transition involves more than vanishing electrical resistance. Unlike the frozen interior magnetic field of a perfect conductor, this equilibrium profile does not retain an arbitrary initial B0​. The Knudsen number is the dimensionless ratio of an intermolecular mean free path ℓmfp​ to a specified characteristic length L of the apparatus or flow. Wall encounters must not be counted as gas–gas collisions in this comparison: doing so would hide the very wall-dominated behavior we want to detect. The same gas can therefore have a small Knudsen number in a large vessel and a large Knudsen number in a tiny opening.

The collision cross-section is πd2, and the 2​ accounts for both partners moving with independent equilibrium velocities. Mixtures and velocity-dependent collision cross-sections require a stated molecular model and mean free path convention; the displayed expression is not an exact formula for every real gas. After isolating the gas supply and pump, keep the bypass open to equalize pressures with the temperature difference already established. Closing the bypass defines t=0. The hot-side pressure rises and the cold-side pressure falls; ultimately their slopes approach zero at unequal pressures. Repeating at different initial pressures changes the degree of rarefaction without changing the microtube. In an idealized reservoir of fixed volume Vi​ and uniform fixed temperature Ti​, the ideal gas law gives N˙i​=[Vi​/(kB​Ti​)]p˙​i​, so opposite inventory changes test particle conservation. If temperature changes, differentiation instead gives N˙i​=(Vi​/kB​)[p˙​i​/Ti​−pi​T˙i​/Ti2​]: a thermal drift can imitate particle transfer. A reproducible pressure split at zero net transfer makes the failure of a single continuum wall model observable, while the Knudsen number organizes which molecular and apparatus scales are competing.

Thermodynamic limit

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Statistical physics OurBigBook.com
The thermodynamic limit describes a sequence of larger systems, not a single enormous specimen: particle number N and volume V tend to infinity with number density n=N/V fixed. Hold the chosen intensive and extensive thermodynamic quantities such as temperature T and an applied magnetic field fixed along that sequence. In the canonical ensemble the controls are T,N,V; in the grand canonical ensemble one instead fixes T and chemical potential, and the limiting number density is a result, possibly with a jump at phase coexistence. These are different specifications of a limiting experiment.
The useful limit is usually an intensive and extensive thermodynamic quantities normalization of the Helmholtz free energy, not a finite limit of the total extensive quantity itself:
FN,V​=−kB​TlogZN,V​,f(T,n)=limN,V→∞N/V=n​​VFN,V​​,a(T,n)=limN,V→∞N/V=n​​NFN,V​​=nf(T,n)​.
(22)
Here ZN,V​ is the canonical partition function, kB​ is the Boltzmann constant, f is free-energy density, and a is Helmholtz free energy per particle. Thus FN,V​=Vf+o(V) when the limit exists; finite systems need not be exactly extensive quantities because of the surface correction to thermodynamic free energy.
Specify the interactions and the growing containers too. For a conventional fluid, use a fixed stable pair potential with a tempered pair potential tail, and containers whose boundary layer of any fixed thickness occupies a vanishing fraction of the volume; uniformly enlarged cubes work, a tube of fixed cross-section does not give the same bulk limit. For a finite-range Ising model, keep the lattice spacing and bond coupling fixed while enlarging all intended spatial directions. Ordinary bounded wall interactions or periodic boundary conditions can then give the same bulk free-energy density, although boundary conditions can select different spontaneous symmetry breaking states. This is a set of hypotheses, not a theorem that every interaction has a boundary-independent limit.[ref]
The Curie–Weiss model below deliberately uses a different limiting prescription: its all-to-all coupling is divided by N. Without that factor its interaction energy would grow as N2, rather than as an extensive quantity. The model has no spatial wall or correlation length to compare with a container; it is an exactly summable illustration of finite-size rounding, not a quantitative model of the fluid experiment below.

Finite-system analyticity (FN​=−kB​TlogZN​)

Thermodynamic limit OurBigBook.com
For finitely many microstates with finite energies Eα​(h) that are real analytic functions of a real control h, the canonical partition function at T>0 is a finite positive sum:
ZN​(T,h)=∑α​e−Eα​(h)/(kB​T)>0.
(23)
It and the resulting Helmholtz free energy are locally real analytic functions of T and h. Hence such a finite Ising model has no literal nonanalytic equilibrium phase transition. A limit of these real analytic functions can nevertheless fail to be a real analytic function; the narrow but smooth crossover can become a sharp phase transition.[ref]
Finite particle number alone is not the hypothesis of a finite sum. Classical phase space is continuous, and a system of quantum states can have infinitely many energy eigenvalues: its partition function requires convergence and local bounds that permit differentiation or an analytic extension of the integral or thermal trace. A divergent partition function, a singularly changed statistical Hamiltonian, or the zero-temperature limit falls outside the finite-positive-sum argument. Observing a steep change in a finite sample therefore motivates a limiting model; it does not measure an actual infinity.

Finite-size rounding replaces a limiting discontinuity or divergence by a finite crossover or peak. For a spatial system near a continuous phase transition, the bulk description ceases to apply unchanged when the correlation length becomes comparable with the sample size. How the crossover width and location depend on size also depends on the model, geometry and boundary conditions; there is no universal 1/N rule for every phase transition.
An exact finite example is the Curie–Weiss model with si​=±1, J>0, and a conjugate field h in energy units. Set K=J/(kB​T) and u=h/(kB​T). Its statistical Hamiltonian and finite partition function are

The binomial coefficient counts the microstates with k positive Ising spins. The diagonal terms in the square add a configuration-independent constant to the energy; retaining them fixes the normalization used here. Divide each summand by ZN​ to obtain the probability mass function of mk​=(2k−N)/N. In particular,

The variance expression makes the finite response nonnegative, while spin inversion symmetry gives ⟨m⟩=0 exactly at u=0 for every plotted N.

For large N well below the critical temperature, their relative Boltzmann weight is approximately e2Num∗​, giving ⟨m⟩≈m∗​tanh(Num∗​). Thus this two-peak approximation has a field width of order 1/(Nm∗​) in u. It is not valid at the critical temperature, where the peaks merge; the figure uses the exact finite sum throughout.

The left panel sketches the measurement principle; the right panel uses deliberately chosen polynomials, Z=1+bx+6x2 with x=nℓ3 and b=±2, where ℓ is a reference length. These curves are not measured data. Their initial slopes have opposite signs, but both bend because of the quadratic term. Using a finite secant from x=0 to x=h gives (Z(h)−1)/h=b+6h, rather than b: reducing the fitting range reduces this particular truncation bias. This algebra explains why measuring one nonideal pressure is insufficient to extract a reliable second virial coefficient.
Waxman and Hastings's 1971 Burnett experiment used sample and expansion chambers in a thermostatic bath, with a valve between them and a pressure transducer linked to a piston gauge. They measured successive isothermal expansions: evacuate the expansion chamber, open the valve, record the equilibrated pressure, isolate and evacuate that chamber again, then repeat. This avoids separately measuring the absolute gas amount and chamber volumes. For carbon dioxide at 50∘C, their measurements below 35 bar gave a molar second virial coefficient of approximately −102.2cm3mol−1. [ref]
An idealized reduction makes the signal explicit. Let q=(VA​+VB​)/VA​ be the calibrated chamber volume ratio, pi​ the pre-expansion pressure, and pf​ the post-expansion pressure. Particle conservation during one valve opening gives nf​=ni​/q. At the same temperature, division of the two equations of state yields
pf​pi​​=qZ(ni​/q,T)Z(ni​,T)​=q+(q−1)kB​TB2​(T)​pi​+O(pi2​).
(30)
Thus the intercept determines q, while the dilute-limit slope determines the second virial coefficient. In the actual experiment, helium runs calibrated the cell constant and chamber deformation corrections were included. Agreement of the carbon dioxide low-pressure intercept with the helium calibration, and the absence of an anomalous low-pressure upturn, checked for gas adsorption on chamber walls. [ref]
For a limited dilute-gas fit, hold temperature fixed, allow thermal equilibrium after every expansion, calibrate absolute pressure and the chamber ratio, and check leaks and sample composition. Repeat the analysis with a smaller upper pressure cutoff and an added curvature term; compare the resulting second virial coefficients with their uncertainties. Too wide a range mixes in higher coefficients; too narrow a range makes the nonideal signal hard to distinguish from instrument error. The displayed chamber equation neglects deformation, dead spaces and adsorption, so it is a teaching reduction rather than the complete experimental analysis.
Units matter. With number density in m−3, B2​ has units m3 and B3​ has units m6. For molar density c=n/NA​ in molm−3, the same equation of state is
Z=cRTp​=1+B2,m​c+B3,m​c2+⋯,B2,m​=NA​B2​,B3,m​=NA2​B3​.
(31)
Here NA​ is the Avogadro constant and R=NA​kB​ is the molar gas constant; the molar coefficients have units m3mol−1 and m6mol−2. A coefficient tabulated per mole must therefore multiply molar density, not number density.
For the classical formulas below, use a nondegenerate gas with thermal de Broglie wavelength λth​ satisfying nλth3​≪1, negligible quantum corrections to relative motion, and a stable, sufficiently short-ranged pair potential. Diluteness must also control the omitted interaction terms: ∣B2​n∣≪1 alone is not enough when positive and negative contributions cancel. A finite truncation is a local low-number density approximation, not an equation of state for a dense liquid or across a phase transition. [ref] [ref]

Second virial coefficient (B2​)

Words: 361
Virial expansion OurBigBook.com
The second virial coefficient is the leading interaction correction to the ideal gas law: at fixed temperature, B2​(T)=limn→0​(Z−1)/n, where Z=p/(nkB​T) and n is number density. For identical classical particles in a homogeneous three-dimensional gas, with an isotropic pair potential u(r) and r the centre-to-centre separation,
B2​(T)=−21​∫R3​f(∣r∣)d3r=2π∫0∞​[1−e−u(r)/(kB​T)]r2dr,f(r)=e−u(r)/(kB​T)−1.
(32)
The function f is the Mayer f-function. The factor 4πr2dr counts the volume of a thin spherical shell; the factor 1/2 counts each unordered pair once. The result has units of volume. Repulsive regions, u>0, contribute positively, while attractive regions, u<0, contribute negatively. [ref]
This is a striking bridge from a microscopic pair potential to a macroscopic pressure reading. At sufficiently small number density, B2​>0 raises pressure relative to an ideal gas at the same temperature and number density, while B2​<0 lowers it. A single value of B2​, however, cannot determine the entire pair potential: many different functions have the same weighted integral. Measurements over several temperatures supply more information.
The integral must exist. For example, a bounded short-range attraction outside a hard core has no difficulty. If instead u(r)∼A/rs as r→∞, then 1−e−u/(kB​T)∼u/(kB​T) and the radial tail behaves like ∫r2−sdr: it converges only for s>3. A bare unscreened Coulomb potential therefore falls outside this formula's ordinary short-range setting. This condition on the tail does not by itself establish the stability or convergence of the full virial expansion.
For an exactly integrable toy attraction, choose the following square-well pair potential, with diameter σ>0, attraction depth ϵ>0, and range multiplier a>1:
u(r)=⎩⎨⎧​+∞,−ϵ,0,​0≤r<σ,σ≤r<aσ,r≥aσ.​
(33)
Set T∗=kB​T/ϵ and bHS​=2πσ3/3, the second virial coefficient of a hard-sphere gas. Integrating the core and attractive shell separately gives the exact toy result
B2​(T)=bHS​[1−(a3−1)(e1/T∗−1)].
(34)
The core contributes bHS​; the shell contributes −bHS​(a3−1)(e1/T∗−1). Heating weakens the relative Boltzmann factor enhancement of attractive configurations, so B2​ approaches the positive hard-core value as T∗→∞. For the illustrative choice a=3/2, the zero occurs at
T0∗​=log(1+a3−11​)1​=log(27/19)1​≈2.846.
(35)
At this temperature, Z=1+B3​n2+⋯: cancellation removes the linear correction, not every correction. At low T∗, the negative shell contribution becomes large, requiring a correspondingly smaller number density for a useful truncated virial expansion. The square well is a deliberately chosen model, not a fit to the carbon dioxide experiment.

Mayer f-function (f(r)=e−u(r)/(kB​T)−1)

Words: 172
Pair potential OurBigBook.com
The Mayer f-function measures how a pair potential changes a pair's Boltzmann factor relative to the noninteracting value one:
f(r)=e−βu(r)−1,β=kB​T1​.
(36)
It vanishes where u=0, lies between −1 and 0 for repulsion, and is positive for attraction. Even an infinite hard-core potential energy produces the finite value f=−1. This is why expanding in Mayer f-functions handles a hard-sphere gas more naturally than a Taylor series in u. [ref]
For pairwise-additive potential energy U=∑i<j​u(rij​), the exact identity
e−βU=∏i<j​[1+f(rij​)]
(37)
turns the configurational part of the canonical partition function into a sum of products associated with pairs. Drawing one edge for each chosen factor f(rij​) gives the graphs used in the cluster expansion. The second virial coefficient uses just one pair's relative-position integral, B2​=−21​∫fd3r.
For the square-well toy pair potential in second virial coefficient, f=−1 in the core, f=e1/T∗−1 in the attractive shell, and f=0 beyond it. Its positive plateau need not be small: low number density, rather than small f at every separation, controls the dilute-gas approximation. The integral weights each plateau by spherical-shell volume; equal-looking unweighted areas on a plot of f versus r need not cancel in B2​.

Hard-sphere gas

Words: 320 Articles: 1
Pair potential OurBigBook.com
A hard-sphere gas is a classical model of identical impenetrable spheres, each of diameter σ and radius σ/2. Its pair potential is u(r)=+∞ for centre separation r<σ and u(r)=0 for r≥σ; the convention at exact contact has no effect on the integral. It isolates the effect of particle size without an attractive potential energy.
The upper-left panel is a cross-section of a three-dimensional forbidden region: the second centre cannot enter a sphere of radius σ around the first centre. The particles themselves have radius σ/2. Consequently, with particle volume vs​ and pair excluded volume vex​,
vs​=34π​(2σ​)3=6πσ3​,vex​=34πσ3​=8vs​,B2​=21​vex​=4vs​=32πσ3​.
(38)
The last equality follows directly from the Mayer f-function: f=−1 throughout the forbidden volume and zero outside it. Confusing particle radius with contact separation changes the answer by a factor of eight; omitting the unordered-pair factor changes it by a further factor of two.
Define the packing fraction η=nvs​, where n is number density. Then the virial expansion begins
nkB​Tp​=1+4η+O(η2).
(39)
For example, at the toy value η=0.01, the leading correction predicts Z≈1.04; the omitted terms still matter if accuracy beyond this approximation is needed. The classical second virial coefficient is independent of temperature because the geometry of forbidden configurations does not change when the gas is warmed. The pressure itself still scales with temperature at fixed number density.
This model makes the positive correction particularly clear: eliminating overlapping configurations changes the dependence of the available configuration space on volume, even though the allowed configurations all have zero interaction energy. The figure's other panels add a toy attractive shell and show how its Boltzmann factor competes with that geometry. The hard-sphere gas is a useful reference model, while a low-order virial expansion remains a dilute-gas approximation rather than a dense sphere packing formula.

At zero field the potential can have two wells, but a finite barrier still permits quantum tunnelling and gives a unique symmetric ground state. The excitation gap produces a finite classical correlation length, so there is no finite-temperature spontaneous magnetization for fixed positive κ. One classical spatial coordinate becomes imaginary time; a d-dimensional classical model corresponds to a quantum model with d−1 spatial dimensions.

The zero-field Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation of an exponentially coupled Ising model produces U(m)=Am2−log[2cosh(2m)], where A=tanh(κ/2)/J>0. Since U′′(0)=2A−4 and U tends to positive infinity, a symmetric double well exists exactly when A<2. Its nonzero stationary points solve Am=tanh(2m); the ratio tanh(2m)/m decreases from 2 to 0 for m>0, proving that there is exactly one positive minimum. At A=2 the minimum is a single quartic minimum. A small conjugate field adds −htanh(2m)+O(h2) and tilts the wells, while a sufficiently large field can remove the metastable well. A finite barrier permits quantum tunnelling; two classical minima alone do not establish spontaneous symmetry breaking.

Ising model OurBigBook.com
A fixed Ising boundary condition pins the Ising spins on a specified boundary, leaving the interior distributed with the original interaction weights. The boundary can be the inner graph vertex boundary of a finite box, or an exterior neighboring set if that convention is explicitly chosen. Conditioning on pinned Ising spins preserves the FKG lattice condition of a ferromagnetic Ising model. The FKG inequality then makes interior expectations of increasing observables nondecreasing in the pinned boundary Ising spins.

The nearest-neighbor spatial conditional probability distribution reduces each domain comparison to a mixture of boundary conditions for the smaller box. Probabilities that a specified finite set is all one consequently converge; inclusion-exclusion gives convergence of every finite Ising spin pattern. Their consistent limits define the two extreme infinite-volume measures. Existence does not assert that the two limits coincide.

Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution (s=kB​T/m​)

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Quantum ideal-gas statistics OurBigBook.com
The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution describes the random velocities and speeds of particles in a classical ideal gas at thermal equilibrium. Individual particles keep changing velocity through collisions, while the equilibrium probability distribution stays fixed. For one species of particle mass m at positive temperature T, the characteristic scale is
s=mkB​T​​,
(54)
where kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. A signed velocity component follows a normal distribution; the nonnegative magnitude follows the Maxwell speed distribution. Their peaks differ because a speed measurement groups together all directions of motion.
Use the gas rest frame, three spatial dimensions, and nonrelativistic particles, with kB​T≪mc2 where c is the speed of light. Assume a dilute gas whose interactions between encounters can be neglected in the ideal gas approximation and whose translational motion is classical. A sufficient condition for negligible quantum exchange effects is nλ3≪1, where n is the number density and λ the thermal de Broglie wavelength. Diluteness alone does not guarantee thermal equilibrium; the gas must have equilibrated. These are the assumptions behind the classical Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution. [ref] [ref]
The connection to Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics is the Boltzmann factor for translational kinetic energy, Ekin​=m∣v∣2/2. Normalizing e−Ekin​/(kB​T) over velocity gives a probability density; an occupation factor e(μ−E)/(kB​T) instead specifies a mean occupation, with chemical potential μ. Their normalizations serve different purposes. [ref]
This connects microscopic motion to measurements: a gas thermometer uses the ideal gas law, collisions and the mean free path govern transport, and measurements of spectral lines use thermal Doppler broadening to infer temperature. Each probes a different aspect of the same thermal motion.
In 1860, James Clerk Maxwell presented the component and speed laws in Part I, Proposition IV of Illustrations of the Dynamical Theory of Gases, pp. 22–23. His argument combined independence of the three velocity components with isotropy, and he explicitly compared the component law with the normal distribution of observational errors. Independence is an assumption of that argument; perpendicular coordinate axes alone do not establish it. [ref]

In the gas rest frame, the Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution is the probability density function per unit volume in velocity space:

(55)
Thus f(v)d3v gives the probability of a small three-dimensional velocity region. For a gas with bulk mean velocity V, replace v by v−V; the Maxwell speed distribution then describes the magnitude relative to that bulk motion.
For any one Cartesian velocity component vx​, integrating out the other two gives
q(vx​)=2π​s1​e−vx2​/(2s2),⟨vx​⟩=0,⟨vx2​⟩=s2=mkB​T​.
(56)
The factorization f(v)=q(vx​)q(vy​)q(vz​) establishes independence: all three components are centered normal random variables, with variance s2. Both the component density q and the vector density f have their largest values at zero. This concerns densities for small equal-sized regions; any single exact velocity still has probability zero. [ref]
The standard deviation s measures thermal motion even though the mean velocity is zero. Positive and negative components cancel in the mean, but their squares add. This is why thermal Doppler broadening measures a nonzero line width in a gas with no bulk motion.

Words: 502 Articles: 1
Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution OurBigBook.com
The Maxwell speed distribution is the probability density function for the magnitude v=∣v∣. Unlike a signed velocity component, speed cannot be negative:
g(v)=4πv2(2πkB​Tm​)3/2e−mv2/(2kB​T)=π2​​s3v2​e−v2/(2s2),v≥0.

For 0≤a<b, the probability of a speed in [a,b] is ∫ab​g(v)dv, and ∫0∞​g(v)dv=1. The density has units of inverse speed, so its height alone is not a probability. [ref]
All velocities with magnitudes from v to v+dv occupy a thin spherical shell of volume 4πv2dv in velocity space. The isotropy of the Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution makes its density constant over each shell, giving g(v)=4πv2f(vex​) for any fixed unit direction ex​. A larger radius offers more directions and more volume. The increasing shell factor initially wins over the decreasing Boltzmann factor, so g(0)=0 and the most probable speed is positive. This is the geometric reason that the peaks of the vector and speed densities disagree.
With the dimensionless quantity u=v/s, every such gas has the same rescaled speed density:
g(v)dv=h(u)du,h(u)=π2​​u2e−u2/2,u≥0.
(58)
For comparison, w=vx​/s has the standard normal distribution density ϕ(w)=e−w2/2/2π​ on the whole real line. The Maxwell speed distribution is neither the positive half of this curve nor the distribution of ∣vx​∣: it combines three components.
The first two moments of the Maxwell speed distribution give the mean and root mean square:
⟨v⟩=π8​​s,⟨v2⟩=3s2,vrms​=⟨v2⟩​=3​s.

Consequently the mean translational kinetic energy is m⟨v2⟩/2=3kB​T/2, as required by the equipartition theorem. [ref] The mean speed weights fast particles more than the density peak does, and the root mean square weights them more strongly still.
Changing temperature or particle mass only changes s∝T/m​. At fixed mass, four times the temperature doubles every characteristic speed; at fixed temperature, four times the mass halves them. A stretched density becomes lower so that its area stays one. For two species at the same temperature, equal mean translational kinetic energy therefore means different typical speeds.

Magnetic susceptibility describes how readily a magnetic field changes a material's magnetization. The field variable and normalization matter: volume magnetic susceptibility in the International System of Units is dimensionless, whereas a derivative of total magnetic moment with respect to B has units of JT−2. A slope measured against the applied magnetic field intensity also depends on the sample's demagnetizing field.
For an isotropic, reversible linear response through the origin, write
M=χv​Hint​,Bint​=μ0​(Hint​+M)=μ0​(1+χv​)Hint​.
(85)
Here M is magnetization, or magnetic moment per volume; Hint​ is the internal magnetic field intensity; Bint​ is the internal magnetic flux density; and μ0​ is the vacuum permeability. Both M and H have units Am−1. The magnetic permeability is μ0​(1+χv​). [ref]
The independent-moment magnetic response below shows why one number cannot describe every field: magnetization approaches a saturation magnetization, while its differential magnetic susceptibility approaches zero. Anisotropy requires a magnetic susceptibility tensor; hysteresis requires specifying the preparation and sweep branch as well as the bias magnetic field, temperature, and timescale. The Gouy balance turns a small response into a measurable force without presuming that its readout is already the intrinsic volume magnetic susceptibility.

Consider a stipulated dilute collection of independent two-level systems, each with longitudinal magnetic moment sμ, s=±1, and energy Es​=−sμB0​. The prescribed vacuum/applied magnetic flux density is B0​=μ0​Happ​. Ignore interactions, orbital magnetic response, and the small sample-field correction. This is the magnetic version of the existing independent spin-one-half two-level system, with alignment probabilities rather than an interacting Curie–Weiss model.
For temperature T>0, the canonical ensemble gives the one-moment partition function Z1​=2coshx, with x=μB0​/(kB​T). Taking the expected value over its two Boltzmann weights gives
⟨s⟩=ex+e−xex−e−x​=tanhx,M=nμtanhx,χmodel​≡(∂Happ​∂M​)T​=kB​Tμ0​nμ2​cosh2x1​.
(91)
Here n is the number density, kB​ the Boltzmann constant, and tanh the hyperbolic tangent. For ∣x∣≪1, its small-argument expansion of the hyperbolic tangent gives M≃μ0​nμ2Happ​/(kB​T), a Curie's law response in the applied-H convention. For large ∣x∣, M approaches the saturation magnetization nμ with sign set by the field, and its differential magnetic susceptibility falls towards zero.
Both plots use stipulated n=1026m−3, μ=9.2740101×10−24JT−1, kB​=1.380649×10−23JK−1, and μ0​=1.25663706×10−6TmA−1. The moment is approximately one Bohr magneton; the chosen vacuum permeability is a rounded model input. At T=2K, Ms​=927.401Am−1 and χmodel​(0)=3.91410×10−4. The linear approximation overestimates M by less than 3% for ∣x∣≤0.3, corresponding to ∣μ0​Happ​∣≤0.89324T or ∣Happ​∣≤0.71082MAm−1. These parameters keep the modeled response weak; neglected magnetic feedback is of relative order χmodel​(0), rather than an explanation of a material's ordered phase.
At B0​=0, cooling increases the zero-field slope as 1/T. At fixed B0​=0, cooling instead gives χmodel​∼4μ0​nμ2e−2μ∣B0​∣/(kB​T)/(kB​T): a saturated moment can hardly change further. The order of the zero-field and zero-temperature limits matters. This independent model has no finite-temperature collective phase transition; the diverging zero-field slope alone does not establish one.

Saturation magnetization is the limiting magnetization when the responding magnetic moments are fully aligned within the stated model or experimental regime. In independent-moment magnetic response, Ms​=nμ. Reaching a large magnetization does not imply a large differential magnetic susceptibility: the remaining slope can be almost zero.

Gouy balance

Words: 341
Magnetic susceptibility OurBigBook.com
A Gouy balance detects the force exerted by a nonuniform magnetic field on a sample of uniform cross-section extending between high- and low-field regions. TeachSpin's implementation reverses the usual arrangement: a rare-earth permanent-magnet assembly sits on a one-pan electronic balance, while a separate holder brings the sample into the field. The magnet's apparent mass change measures the opposite of the sample's vertical force, by Newton's third law. The described pole faces have diameter 25mm and separation 15mm; samples occupy cuvettes of cross-section (10mm)2 and height about 32mm. [ref]
The same balance calibrates magnetic flux density by measuring the reaction force on the magnet when a wire of known horizontal length L carries known electric current i perpendicular to the field: ∣Fz​∣=iLB0​. The manufacturer describes water being repelled by the high-field region, identifying negative magnetic susceptibility. This observed sign supplies a qualitative test, not a measured Curie's law curve. [ref]
For weak reversible linear response, a uniform sample displacing a weakly magnetic surrounding medium has, to leading order, downward force
F↓​≃2μ0​A(χv​−χmedium​)​(B0,bottom2​−B0,top2​).
(92)
This follows by integrating the induced-dipole force density (χv​−χmedium​)∂z​(B02​)/(2μ0​) along a downward coordinate. A is the cross-sectional area, and the two B0​ values are applied magnetic flux densities. The force depends on the endpoint fields; the entire field-gradient profile need not be measured under these assumptions. In the reversed apparatus, F↓​=−gΔmmagnet​ after subtracting the holder background, where g is gravitational acceleration. This sign must be reversed before inferring volume magnetic susceptibility.
Useful controls are an empty-holder reading at the same position, a distant-sample baseline, repeated wire-current reversals during field calibration, and stable temperature. They separate holder response, balance drift, force offsets, and thermal changes; these are proposed checks for the stated inference. Finite endpoint fields, nonuniform cross-section, uneven powder packing, stray forces and a demagnetizing field limit the simple formula. If magnetization is nonlinear, the weak-response force involves A∫B0,top​B0,bottom​​M(B0​)dB0​ instead of a constant-χv​ endpoint square. A balance reading then measures an integrated response, not directly the local differential magnetic susceptibility.

Planck's law (Bν​(T), Bλ​(T))

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Statistical physics OurBigBook.com
Planck's law gives the spectral radiance of an ideal blackbody in thermal equilibrium at absolute temperature T>0. It predicts how much power is carried in each small frequency or wavelength interval, per projected area and per solid angle. The whole curve is determined by T: no material-specific parameter enters this ideal Planck function.
Writing ν for frequency in hertz and λ for wavelength in metres, the two forms of the Planck function are
Bν​(T)=c22hν3​ehν/(kB​T)−11​,Bλ​(T)=λ52hc2​ehc/(λkB​T)−11​.
(93)
Here h is the Planck constant, kB​ the Boltzmann constant, and c the speed of light in vacuum. Their exact values in the International System of Units are h=6.62607015×10−34Js, kB​=1.380649×10−23JK−1, and c=299792458ms−1. [ref]
The units matter: Bν​ is measured in Wm−2sr−1Hz−1, whereas Bλ​ is measured in Wm−2sr−1m−1. Both are spectral radiance, rather than radiant exitance or energy density. To report Bλ​ per micrometre, multiply its per-metre value by 10−6; a micrometre-wide interval is 10−6 metres wide.
For a computed example, at T=6000K and λ=0.500μm, the exponent is hc/(λkB​T)≈4.79592. Substitution into Planck's law gives Bλ​≈3.17569×1013Wm−2sr−1m−1, or 3.17569×107Wm−2sr−1 per micrometre. At the same wavelength, the illustrative temperatures 3000K and 4500K give 2.60268×105 and 6.37793×106 in the latter units. These are ideal predictions for stipulated temperatures.
The key change of variables is ν=c/λ. Corresponding positive intervals carry the same power, so Bλ​dλ=Bν​∣dν∣ and
Bλ​(T)=Bν​(T)​ν=c/λ​λ2c​.
(94)
Equal-width wavelength intervals have unequal widths in frequency; the factor c/λ2 compensates for this. Merely replacing the horizontal-axis labels of Bν​ by c/ν does not produce Bλ​. This explains the frequency and wavelength peaks of Planck's law.
A short derivation uses the Boltzmann distribution for a single electromagnetic mode with thermal energies nhν, n=0,1,…. Put q=e−hν/(kB​T). The geometric series gives Z=∑n≥0​qn=(1−q)−1 and mean thermal energy hνq/(1−q). The electromagnetic mode density in a box, including both independent polarization of an electromagnetic wave states of a photon, is 8πν2/c3 per volume per unit frequency. Multiplication gives spectral energy density uν​=8πhν3/[c3(ehν/(kB​T)−1)]; isotropy gives Bν​=cuν​/(4π). This counts thermal excitation energy, excluding zero-point energy. [ref]
Planck's law connects quantum mechanics to a measurable radiation curve. Its small-hν/(kB​T) limit is the Rayleigh-Jeans law, Bν​≈2kB​Tν2/c2; its large-hν/(kB​T) limit is the Wien approximation, Bν​≈(2hν3/c2)e−hν/(kB​T). The suppression at high frequency makes the total energy density finite. Integrating the curve gives the Stefan–Boltzmann law, while locating its peak gives Wien's displacement law. Thus one formula predicts both the spectral shape and the total emission.

Frequency and wavelength peaks of Planck's law (λmax​T=b,νmax​/T=xν​kB​/h)

Words: 304
Planck's law OurBigBook.com
At a fixed temperature, the frequency maximizing Bν​ and the wavelength maximizing Bλ​ in Planck's law are different ways of describing the same black-body radiation. They are maxima of different densities. The inverse relation between frequency and wavelength does not preserve those maxima because its interval-conversion factor varies with wavelength.
For a short extremum calculation, substitute x=hν/(kB​T) into Bν​, leaving a positive constant times x3/(ex−1). Substitute x=hc/(λkB​T) into Bλ​, leaving a positive constant times x5/(ex−1). Setting each derivative to zero gives
3(1−e−xν​)=xν​,5(1−e−xλ​)=xλ​.
(95)
Select the positive roots: xν​=2.821439372… and xλ​=4.965114232…. Although x=0 solves the rearranged equations, it is an endpoint, not either peak. For m=3 or 5, the function m(1−e−x)−x initially increases, its derivative me−x−1 crosses zero once, and it eventually becomes negative. Hence it has exactly one positive root. Each density tends to zero at both ends, so this root gives its unique maximum. The bisection method brackets these roots in (1,3) and (1,5).
Consequently Wien's displacement law gives
λmax​T=kB​xλ​hc​=b≈2.897771955×10−3mK,Tνmax​​=hkB​xν​​≈5.878925758×1010HzK−1.
(96)
These constants agree with NIST's tabulation. [ref] The wavelength peaks at 3000, 4500, and 6000K are 965.924, 643.949, and 482.962nm. Doubling temperature halves this peak wavelength.
At 6000K, the frequency peak is νmax​≈352.736THz, whose converted wavelength is c/νmax​≈0.849907μm. The Bλ​ peak is instead 0.482962μm, corresponding to about 620.737THz. These numbers are compatible: equal-width frequency bins and equal-width wavelength bins partition the same radiation differently. Specifying which density was maximized is essential when using a peak to infer temperature.

Black-body radiation (u=arad​T4,p=u/3)

Words: 426 Articles: 2
Planck's law OurBigBook.com
Black-body radiation is the electromagnetic radiation in thermal equilibrium with an ideal blackbody. It can be described as a photon gas: a cavity whose walls are all at the same temperature contains radiation with the universal Planck's law spectrum. A small opening in such a cavity approximates a blackbody emitter because incoming radiation undergoes repeated absorption inside. The radiation's equilibrium spectrum depends on temperature, rather than the wall material. [ref]
There are three useful quantities to keep distinct: directional spectral radiance Bν​ or Bλ​, total energy density u in the cavity, and outward radiant exitance j∗ from its opening. Planck's law supplies the first; integrals over frequency and directions supply the others. For isotropy, every direction has the same Bν​, so the full 4π solid angle gives
u(T)=c4π​∫0∞​Bν​(T)dν=arad​T4,arad​=15h3c38π5kB4​​=15ℏ3c3π2kB4​​.
(100)
Here ℏ=h/(2π) is the reduced Planck constant, and the radiation constant is arad​≈7.565733250×10−16Jm−3K−4. The explicit Boltzmann constant makes this an SI formula; adopting natural units with kB​=1 recovers u=π2T4/(15ℏ3c3).
For a short integral outline, substitute x=hν/(kB​T) and use
∫0∞​ex−1x3​dx=∑n=1∞​∫0∞​x3e−nxdx=6∑n=1∞​n41​=15π4​.
(101)
The expansion is a geometric series with nonnegative terms; repeated integration by parts evaluates each integral, and ζ(4)=π4/90 is a value of the Riemann zeta function. This gives the coefficient above.
The photon gas also exerts radiation pressure, p=u/3. The factor 1/3 comes from the angular average of the squared directional component of photon momentum, ⟨cos2θ⟩=1/3. The thermodynamic derivation of blackbody radiation pressure gives the same result. In contrast, outgoing power involves one projected-direction factor over an outward hemisphere, yielding radiant exitance
j∗=π∫0∞​Bν​(T)dν=4cu​=σT4,σ=15h3c22π5kB4​​.
(102)
This is the Stefan–Boltzmann law with unit emissivity; σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. The factor π follows from Lambert's cosine law, rather than the 4π full-sphere factor used for energy density.
For example, an ideal 6000K cavity has u≈0.980519Jm−3, radiation pressure p≈0.326840Pa, and outward radiant exitance j∗≈7.34881×107Wm−2. A stipulated 3000K cavity has one-sixteenth each value because all three scale as T4. These describe stored energy, mechanical pressure, and outgoing power per area, respectively. In a closed equilibrium cavity, equal opposing radiation balances the directional power flow even though u and p are nonzero.
The usefulness of black-body radiation is this common reference: Planck's law, Wien's displacement law, and the Stefan–Boltzmann law consistently connect spectral measurements, temperature, and total emission. The three illustrative curves in Planck's law are ideal equilibrium spectra; applying them to a material requires considering its emissivity and whether thermal equilibrium is a suitable approximation.

Canonical ensemble (ps​=Z−1e−βEs​)

Words: 2k Articles: 23
Statistical physics OurBigBook.com
The canonical ensemble is the probability distribution for a system in thermal equilibrium with a heat bath at fixed temperature T, with fixed particle number and external parameters. It allows energy exchange, so individual energy measurements fluctuate. With Boltzmann constant kB​ and inverse temperature β=1/(kB​T),
ps​=Ze−βEs​​,Z=∑s​e−βEs​.
(109)
The heat bath is idealized as large enough that exchanges barely change its temperature; coupling must permit equilibration while contributing negligible interaction energy. A finite heat bath approximates this description only when its temperature change is negligible over the relevant exchanges. Strong coupling or a small heat bath can require a different description.
For one two-level system at positive temperature, the Boltzmann weights are 1,e−βΔ, hence
Z1​=1+e−βΔ,p=Z1​e−βΔ​=1+eβΔ1​.
(110)
At βΔ=ln3, Z1​=4/3 and p=1/4. This is a probabilistic thermal mixed state. For quantum levels, its density matrix is ρ=(1−p)∣0⟩⟨0∣+p∣1⟩⟨1∣. The pure state 1−p​∣0⟩+p​∣1⟩ has the same energy measurement probabilities, but also has quantum coherence between the energy eigenstates. Matching those probabilities does not make the states equivalent.

Canonical partition function (Z(β))

Words: 537 Articles: 12
Canonical ensemble OurBigBook.com
The partition function Z(β)=∑s​e−βEs​ is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over individual microstates. Dividing by it makes their probabilities sum to one. When summing distinct energies instead, include the state degeneracy: Z=∑E​g(E)e−βE. For two independent distinguishable two-level systems,
Z2​=1+2e−βΔ+e−2βΔ=Z12​.
(111)
The middle coefficient counts two microstates, exactly as in the preceding figure. For N such units, ZN​=Z1N​; this factorization requires additive energy and independence, and generally fails with interactions.
The usefulness goes beyond normalization. For fixed energies, derivatives of the natural logarithm of the partition function yield measurable quantities:
U=⟨E⟩=−∂β​lnZ,Var(E)=∂β2​lnZ,S=kB​(lnZ+βU).
(112)
Here U is internal energy, the second expression is the energy variance, and S is Gibbs entropy. For one two-level system at fixed Δ, its heat capacity C=∂U/∂T and entropy are
U=Δp,kB​C​=(1+eβΔ)2(βΔ)2eβΔ​,kB​S​=ln(1+e−βΔ)+βΔp.
(113)
At βΔ=ln3, these give U/Δ=0.25, C/kB​≃0.2263 and S/kB​≃0.5623. For independent units, all three quantities add.
The figure shows why heat capacity peaks. At low temperature, the excited energy is rarely occupied; at high temperature, the probabilities are almost equal and further warming barely changes internal energy. The largest response lies between these limits, at kB​T/Δ≃0.4168, where C/kB​≃0.4392. Meanwhile entropy rises from zero toward kB​ln2, reflecting two equally likely alternatives. This high-temperature limit belongs to the stipulated two-level system; extra accessible energy eigenstates would change it.

The equipartition theorem says that each independent quadratic term in a Hamiltonian described by classical mechanics has mean energy kB​T/2 in a canonical ensemble. Here kB​ is the Boltzmann constant and T>0 the absolute temperature. Count terms in the energy, rather than vaguely counting everything that can move: one harmonic oscillator has one position degree of freedom but TWO quadratic terms, one in momentum and one in displacement.
A precise sufficient setting is H(y,ξ)=ay2/2+H0​(ξ) with a>0, where y is one of the canonical variables, ξ denotes all remaining variables, and the phase space integration measure factors as dydξ. The range of y is the whole real line, independently of ξ; there is no constraint coupling its allowed values to other variables. The partition function must be finite, and the relevant expected values must exist. The Boltzmann factor then gives
β=kB​T1​,ρy​(y)=2πβa​​e−βay2/2,⟨2ay2​⟩=2kB​T​.
(131)
The probability density function ρy​ is a normal distribution with variance kB​T/a. A larger coefficient narrows the fluctuations enough to cancel its greater energy cost. This is why the mean contribution is independent of mass or spring constant.[ref]
For a proof outline, the one-variable Gaussian integral is Zy​=∫−∞∞​e−βay2/2dy=2π/(βa)​, so −∂β​lnZy​=1/(2β). More generally, integration by parts in a canonical variable gives ⟨y∂y​H⟩=kB​T when its boundary term [ye−βH] vanishes and the integrals converge. For ay2/2 this is twice its mean energy. At a finite hard boundary the boundary term need not vanish; hard-wall correction to harmonic equipartition illustrates the resulting departure. A constraint, a nonquadratic potential energy, or a noncanonical integration measure therefore requires its own calculation. The theorem is an ensemble average, not equality of instantaneous energies, and applying it to a recorded trajectory requires equilibration and sufficient sampling.
For a classical one-dimensional harmonic oscillator, with positive mass m and spring constant k,
H=2mp2​+2kx2​,2m⟨p2⟩​=2k⟨x2⟩​=2kB​T​,⟨H⟩=kB​T.
(132)
The origin is the equilibrium position. Its heat capacity is kB​ at fixed m,k, not kB​/2. Although the two mean energies agree, their measured amplitudes do not: ⟨p2⟩=mkB​T and ⟨x2⟩=kB​T/k. In a harmonic optical trap, the position measurement observes the potential energy contribution; it does not measure both contributions by observing x alone.[ref]
For N particles in a three-dimensional classical monatomic gas, neglect interactions and thermally accessible internal excitations. Its three translational momentum terms give internal energy U=3NkB​T/2, heat capacity at constant volume CV​=3NkB​/2, and heat capacity at constant pressure Cp​=CV​+NkB​=5NkB​/2. Per mole, replace NkB​ by the molar gas constant R. For example, using stipulated R=8.314Jmol−1K−1, the molar heat capacity at fixed volume is 12.471Jmol−1K−1. These results assume a dilute, nonrelativistic ideal gas with classical translational statistics, rather than a quantum degeneracy regime.
For an ideal gas of diatomic molecules, modeled as two chemical atoms with a bond, there are three translational quadratic terms, two accessible rotational kinetic energy terms for changes of bond orientation, and one bond-stretching harmonic oscillator with two quadratic terms. Rotation about the bond axis is not an additional active mode in this linear-molecule model. The three familiar limits of heat capacity at constant volume are
NkB​CV​​≃⎩⎨⎧​3/2,5/2,7/2,​rotations and vibrations frozen,rotations active, vibrations frozen,rotations and vibrations classical.​
(133)
Corresponding molar heat capacities are 3R/2, 5R/2 and 7R/2. Counting the stretching harmonic oscillator only once as kB​T/2 would give the wrong last value.[ref]
The frozen regimes require quantum mechanics. In the simple molecular rotation model, Ej​=kB​θr​j(j+1) with state degeneracy 2j+1, θr​=ℏ2/(2IkB​), and moment of inertia I. For the bond-stretching quantum harmonic oscillator, θv​=ℏω/kB​ with angular frequency ω and ℏ=h/(2π) from the Planck constant. When θr​≪θv​, the three limits above correspond to T≪θr​, θr​≪T≪θv​, and T≫θv​, provided translational motion remains classical. They are smooth crossovers, not abrupt switches. Real molecules can have different allowed rotational populations; at high temperature, thermal dissociation, internal excitations and nonharmonic bond motion can invalidate the fixed-molecule model before its last limit is reached.[ref]
For a quantum harmonic oscillator with fixed ω, put z=θv​/T. Its exact mean energy and heat capacity are
⟨H⟩=2ℏω​+ez−1ℏω​,kB​Cosc​​=(1−e−z)2z2e−z​.
(134)
At T≫θv​, the mean energy approaches kB​T and Cosc​ approaches kB​. At T≪θv​, thermal excitation is exponentially suppressed and Cosc​ tends to zero, although the zero-point energy ℏω/2 survives. Frozen thus means little thermal response, not zero motion or zero energy.[ref]
A motivating measurement is thermal calibration of an optical trap. A focused laser through a microscope objective confines a bead in water; imaging or a quadrant photodetector records a position time series. Gieseler and colleagues describe a polystyrene bead of radius 1.03μm at 293.15K, a 1064nm trapping laser, and photodetector acquisition at 105Hz. Their recorded bead continues undergoing Brownian motion; higher trapping power produces a narrower equilibrium position distribution. Infer the centered variance, not a squared distance from an arbitrary camera origin:
σx2​=⟨(x−⟨x⟩)2⟩,k=σx2​kB​T​.
(135)
The normal distribution position histogram and agreement with dynamical calibration methods support the local harmonic optical trap interpretation. For a stipulated example, T=300K and σx​=20nm imply k≃1.04×10−5N/m=0.0104pN/nm. This calculated scale is not an experimental reading.[ref]
Position calibration is essential: if detector output v has conversion x=s(v−v0​), its physical variance is s2Var(v). An unknown scale s cannot be determined together with k from that one variance. A complementary calibration demonstrated by Tolić-Nørrelykke and colleagues combines the power spectrum of thermal motion with the bead response to known sinusoidal motion of a translation stage. The driven response supplies an additional length scale, and their method does not require bead size, liquid dynamic viscosity or wall distance as inputs. It still uses a thermal dynamical model; agreement between methods is a consistency check, not a theory-free proof of equipartition theorem.[ref]
The readout itself can hide fluctuations. Wong and Halvorsen used a 1064nm optical trap and adjustable-exposure CCD imaging of a bead in water. They varied exposure and trapping power, held the bead away from the nearest wall, adjusted illumination to maintain comparable images, and measured tracking noise using a stuck bead. The measured variance fell as exposure increased; corrected results agreed with their time-averaging model. For a stationary overdamped harmonic optical trap, with optical trap relaxation time τ, an exposure of length W measures xˉW​=W−1∫0W​x(t)dt. Its ideal noise-free variance is
Var(xˉW​)=kkB​T​S(α),α=τW​,S(α)=α22(α−1+e−α)​.
(136)
For α>0, S(α)<1: using the blurred variance in the uncorrected formula overestimates k by 1/S(α). At W=τ, the calculated factor is e/2≃1.36. Additive tracking noise instead raises the measured variance and biases the inferred k downward if left uncorrected.[ref]
Useful controls are to record over many optical trap relaxation times, compare blocks for drift, calibrate the position scale, measure fixed-bead noise, vary exposure, and check the position histogram for departures from a normal distribution. A sparse sequence of accurate instantaneous positions can estimate an equilibrium variance; a long exposure averages away motion even if many frames are collected. Flow, appreciable laser heating, escape from the harmonic region or nonconservative forces can break the assumed thermal equilibrium. Inferring k by imposing equipartition theorem is a calibration, whereas testing the relation requires an independently established stiffness and position scale. The beautiful practical connection is that microscopic randomness can set a force scale: once calibrated, a small constant applied force displaces the mean by f/k. The same quadratic-term counting predicts macroscopic heat capacity and makes microscopic fluctuations useful measurements.

Statistical physics OurBigBook.com
Quantum magnetism studies collective phases and excitations of interacting quantum spins.

Geometrical frustration

Words: 49
Quantum magnetism OurBigBook.com
Geometric frustration occurs when the interaction graph prevents all local preferred configurations from being satisfied simultaneously. Antiferromagnetic spins can be antiparallel on every bond of a bipartite graph, but three equal spins on a triangle instead minimize their total exchange by summing to zero, giving a coplanar 120-degree arrangement.

Hubbard model (H=Hhop​+UH​∑n​nn↑​nn↓​)

Words: 265 Articles: 5
Quantum magnetism OurBigBook.com
A lattice fermion model combining hopping with local density interaction, conventionally written UH​∑n​nn↑​nn↓​. Its interaction parameter must be matched when a spin-square representation is used: −2U(S2−3n/4) equals 3Un↑​n↓​, so UH​=3U for that representation.

Words: 42
Hubbard model OurBigBook.com
For a single spinful fermion orbital, S2=3(n−2n↑​n↓​)/4. The contraction term is 3n/4, so :S2:=S2−3n/4=−3n↑​n↓​/2. Empty and doubly occupied states are spinless while singly occupied states have spin one half, which also proves the identity directly.

Itinerant ferromagnetism (ϵkσ​=ϵk​−σM)

Words: 185 Articles: 3
Hubbard model OurBigBook.com
Ferromagnetic spin polarization carried by mobile electrons rather than a separate fixed-spin lattice. A homogeneous spin field splits the electron bands and competes with a positive field cost. Mean-field instability is governed by the Stoner criterion; the ordered metal supports transverse spin waves as well as fermionic particle-hole excitations.
Mean-field itinerant ferromagnetic Goldstone mode (Eq​∼Dq2)
Words: 47
Itinerant ferromagnetism OurBigBook.com
An isotropic spin-polarized metal has a degenerate magnetization direction and a long-wavelength transverse magnon with quadratic dispersion. Nonzero spin density pairs the two transverse broken generators into one type-B Goldstone boson. Exchange-split Fermi surfaces also support fermionic low-energy excitations; the magnon is distinct from longitudinal amplitude motion and the spin-flip continuum.
Stoner criterion (Uc​χ0​=1,χ0​=∫ν(−nF′​)dϵ)
Words: 49
Itinerant ferromagnetism OurBigBook.com
In the homogeneous spin-vector mean-field scheme with field cost M2/(2U) and spin-summed density of states per site, the paramagnetic curvature is proportional to U−1−∫ν(ϵ)[−nF′​(ϵ)]dϵ. It changes sign at Uχ0​=1. For a smooth low-temperature density of states, χ0​≃ν(μ), giving the familiar Fermi-level criterion. Interaction and spin-counting conventions must be specified before comparing coefficients.
Homogeneous spin-field effective action (Seff​=βNM2/(2U)−∑kσ​ln[1+e−β(ϵk​−μ−σM)])
Words: 41
Itinerant ferromagnetism OurBigBook.com
Integrating free fermions in a constant auxiliary spin field gives Seff​=βNM2/(2U)−∑kσ​ln[1+e−β(ϵk​−μ−σM)]. Differentiation gives the self-consistent spin polarization. The extensive action is a mean-field restriction of the full auxiliary-field functional integral, not an exact omission of all spatial/time fluctuations.

The coordination number z is the number of nearest neighbors of a lattice site. A Kac normalization divides a pair coupling by z so that the interaction energy per site remains finite as z→∞.

A Néel state is a two-sublattice product state with antiparallel spin polarization on the two sublattices. It is the classical ordered reference state of a bipartite antiferromagnet.

The Néel order parameter is the slowly varying staggered magnetization of an antiferromagnet. On a bipartite lattice it changes sign between neighboring sublattices before coarse graining.
Quantum depletion of Néel order (Ms​=S−N−1∑k​vk2​)
Words: 63
Néel order parameter OurBigBook.com
For a linear spin-wave approximation, the ground state is empty of the diagonal quasiparticles but contains the original spin bosons. If ak​=uk​αk​−vk​α−k†​, their occupation number is vk2​. The staggered magnetization is reduced from S to S−N−1∑k​vk2​. For the one-dimensional nearest-neighbor Heisenberg antiferromagnet, vk2​=(∣sink∣−1−1)/2 and the integral diverges logarithmically. This invalidates finite ordered magnetization within the approximation; it is not itself a determination of the exact spectral gap.

The staggered magnetization weights the local magnetization with opposite signs on the two sublattices of a bipartite graph. It is nonzero in a Néel state even when the uniform magnetization vanishes.

The uniform magnetization is the nonalternating component of local spin polarization. In a nearly Néel-ordered antiferromagnet it describes the small canting shared by the two sublattices.

Long-range order means that an appropriate connected or symmetry-resolved correlation remains nonzero at arbitrarily large separation. It cannot be created from a product state by a bounded-depth circuit of bounded-range gates.

An antiferromagnetic spin wave is a long-wavelength fluctuation of staggered magnetic order. In an isotropic ordered antiferromagnet its low-energy dispersion is linear.

For a nearest-neighbour Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a hypercubic lattice, the linear spin-wave approximation gives γk​=d−1∑j​cos(kj​a) and the displayed frequency. Near a gapless point its spin-wave velocity is 2JSad​. Its ground-state boson occupation is [1/1−γk2​​−1]/2, producing quantum depletion of Néel order. Exact zero modes need an infrared regulator or separate global-rotation treatment.

A Fermi liquid is an interacting fermion phase whose low-energy excitations are long-lived quasiparticles near a Fermi surface. Its effective interactions are classified by scaling only the frequency and momentum normal to that surface.

A Fermi surface is the codimension-one surface in momentum space separating occupied and unoccupied zero-temperature states of a fermionic system.

Fermi-surface renormalization-group scaling sends frequency and normal displacement from the Fermi surface to zero while leaving tangential momentum fixed. Generic interactions are irrelevant, while forward-scattering and opposite-momentum Cooper channels can remain marginal.

BCS theory OurBigBook.com
A Cooper pair is a correlated pair of fermions associated with superconductivity. The conventional BCS ground state uses opposite-momentum, opposite-spin pair creation operators ck↑†​c−k↓†​. Their total momentum is zero for every relative momentum k; zero total momentum does not restrict k to zero.

BCS ground state (∏k​(uk​+vk​ck↑†​c−k↓†​)∣0⟩)

BCS theory OurBigBook.com
The BCS ground state is the normalized product of empty and occupied pair states ∏k​(uk​+vk​bk†​)∣0⟩. For uk2​+vk2​=1, each pair factor is normalized. The inverse Bogoliubov transformation annihilates it, so it is the vacuum of positive-energy quasiparticles. Although individual factors use opposite momenta, k runs over the relative pair momenta; it is not restricted to k=0.

BCS theory OurBigBook.com
For real gap and the particle-hole block (ξk​−Δk​​−Δk​−ξk​​), the BCS coherence factors obey uk2​=(1+ξk​/Ek​)/2, vk2​=(1−ξk​/Ek​)/2 and uk​vk​=Δk​/(2Ek​), where Ek​=ξk2​+Δk2​​. They diagonalize the Bogoliubov--de Gennes Hamiltonian and give the empty/pair amplitudes of the BCS ground state. Their relative sign depends on the pairing convention.

The BCS anomalous average is the pair expectation ⟨bk​⟩=⟨c−k↓​ck↑​⟩. In the BCS ground state it is uk​vk​=Δk​/(2Ek​) for real gap at zero temperature. At temperature T it becomes Δk​tanh(Ek​/(2kB​T))/(2Ek​). Substitution into the pairing-field definition gives the BCS gap equation.

BCS theory OurBigBook.com
The reduced BCS pairing Hamiltonian retains scattering of opposite-momentum, opposite-spin Cooper pairs:
H=∑k,σ​ϵk​ckσ†​ckσ​+∑k,k′​Vk,k′​bk†​bk′​,bk†​=ck↑†​c−k↓†​.
(141)
A mean-field approximation introduces the BCS anomalous average and pairing field Δk​=−∑k′​Vk,k′​⟨bk′​⟩. The subtraction −∑Vk,k′​⟨bk†​⟩⟨bk′​⟩ corrects the double counting of the mean-field interaction energy.

At zero temperature and weak coupling, the BCS gap equation gives Δ≃2Λe−1/(νF​∣V∣). Its exponential scale agrees with the renormalization-group scale of the Cooper instability.

BCS gap equation OurBigBook.com
An attractive interaction Vk,k′​=−V/V within ∣ξk​∣,∣ξk′​∣<ΩD​ gives a constant gap inside that energy shell and zero outside. With approximately constant single-spin density of states νs​ per volume,
1=νs​V∫0ΩD​​ξ2+Δ2​dξ​=νs​Varsinh(ΩD​/Δ),Δ=sinh(1/(νs​V))ΩD​​.

The weak coupling limit is Δ≃2ΩD​e−1/(νs​V). A density counting both spin species is twice νs​ and must be divided by two. The shell cutoff is a relative-energy condition, even when every Cooper pair has zero total momentum.
